title: Arbitration and Conciliation Act s. 5 — Statutory provision (ACA s. 5)

content.overview: Section 5 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 establishes the principle of limited judicial intervention in matters governed by Part I: notwithstanding other law, judicial authorities shall not intervene except where the Act itself provides for intervention.
content.glance: Section 5 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 establishes the principle of limited judicial intervention in matters governed by Part I: notwithstanding other law, judicial authorities shall not intervene except where the Act itself provides for intervention.
content.study:
1. Non-intervention is the statutory starting point: Section 5 begins with an overriding clause: notwithstanding other law in force, judicial intervention is excluded in matters governed by Part I except where Part I provides for it. The provision therefore gives primacy to the statutory arbitration framework for the question of intervention.

2. Identify whether Part I governs the matter: The phrase “matters governed by this Part” is central. Before invoking section 5, identify the arbitration and procedural setting and determine whether the requested judicial action falls within Part I. The section should not be applied without first establishing its field of operation.

3. Identify the statutory gateway: Section 5 does not list every permissible court intervention. Instead, it makes intervention lawful where Part I provides for it. The application must therefore identify the specific Part I provision that authorises the requested judicial action.

4. Relationship with other laws: The opening non obstante clause means that, in a matter governed by Part I, another law cannot be used as an independent basis for judicial intervention contrary to the Part I scheme. The precise interaction depends on the statutory provision and subject matter actually before the court.

5. Scope of the principle: Section 5 is a rule of statutory allocation of judicial intervention, not a command that courts never act in arbitration matters. Where Part I expressly provides a judicial role, that role remains available. Where no Part I gateway exists, the court must not create intervention merely from general jurisdictional powers.

examples.title: Intervention expressly provided by Part I
examples.body: A party seeks a judicial remedy that Part I expressly assigns to a court. Section 5 does not bar the remedy because the intervention is authorised by the Act itself.

examples.title: Intervention without a Part I gateway
examples.body: A party asks a court to intervene in an arbitral matter but cannot identify a Part I provision authorising that intervention. Section 5 requires the request to be tested against the statutory scheme rather than a general invitation to supervise the arbitration.

examples.title: Reliance on another statute
examples.body: A party invokes another law as the basis for court intervention in a matter governed by Part I. Section 5 requires the court to consider the non obstante clause and whether Part I itself provides the relevant intervention.

hypotheticals.question: A party asks a court to intervene in an arbitration but cites no Part I provision authorising the intervention. Is section 5 automatically satisfied merely because the matter concerns arbitration?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. The applicant must identify the statutory basis for judicial intervention within Part I. Section 5 is not merely a label for arbitration-related disputes; it directs attention to the intervention expressly provided by the statutory scheme.

hypotheticals.question: A party invokes a general power under another law to obtain judicial intervention in a matter governed by Part I. What is the section 5 inquiry?
hypotheticals.analysis: The court must first examine the non obstante clause and determine whether the requested intervention is one that Part I provides for. The general provision cannot be treated as an independent route that bypasses the Part I scheme.

hypotheticals.question: Does section 5 mean that courts have no role once arbitration begins?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Part I itself provides specified judicial functions. Section 5 limits intervention to those statutory gateways; it does not eliminate the judicial role created by Part I.

distinctions.title: Section 5 limitation vs complete judicial exclusion

rows.left: No intervention except where Part I provides for it.
rows.right: Courts can never intervene in arbitration.

rows.left: Judicial gateways remain where the Act expressly provides them.
rows.right: Would improperly erase statutory court functions.

distinctions.title: Part I gateway vs general jurisdiction

rows.right: Cannot bypass the Part I scheme merely because it is a general power.

misconceptions.trap: Section 5 means courts can never intervene in arbitration.
misconceptions.correction: The prohibition is expressly subject to intervention provided for in Part I.

misconceptions.trap: Any arbitration-related application is barred unless the court finds a special exception outside the Act.
misconceptions.correction: The relevant question is whether Part I itself provides the judicial intervention.

misconceptions.trap: A general statutory power can always be used despite section 5.
misconceptions.correction: In a matter governed by Part I, the non obstante clause requires the requested intervention to be tested against the Part I scheme.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What is the governing test under section 5?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: First identify whether the matter is governed by Part I. Then identify the precise judicial intervention sought and the Part I provision that expressly provides for it. If no such statutory gateway exists, section 5 bars the intervention.
questionsAndAnswers.explanation: The section allocates judicial intervention through the statutory scheme.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a section 5 objection be pleaded?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: State the matter and procedural stage, identify the judicial intervention sought, demonstrate that Part I governs the matter, and require the opposing party to identify the Part I provision authorising the intervention. Address the non obstante clause and explain why a general power under another law cannot displace the statutory scheme.
questionsAndAnswers.explanation: The submission should focus on statutory allocation rather than broad assertions of arbitral autonomy.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should ACA section 5 be applied?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Identify the statutory trigger, conditions, exceptions and consequence and apply them to the facts.

examTips: Identify the Part I field of operation.
Name the exact judicial intervention sought.
Identify the Part I gateway authorising it.
Do not describe section 5 as an absolute ouster of courts.
